drop.title: The Primes That Split in Two

title: The Primes That
Split in Two
slides.dek: Ask any odd prime whether it is a sum of two squares. Half of them are, half never can be, and Fermat found the tell in 1640: it is decided by the single digit you get from dividing by four. Run the rule live, watch a circle hunt for a lattice point, then follow it out to Lagrange's promise that four squares is always enough.

slides.body: Take any odd prime and try to write it as two squares added together. 13 = 2² + 3². 5 = 1² + 2². Now try 7, or 11, or 19: you will never find it, because there is nothing to find. Some primes split cleanly in two; some refuse, forever. *Pierre de Fermat* stated the tell in a letter of 1640, so plainly that *Euler* needed the better part of seven years to prove it (finished around 1749): an odd prime is a sum of two squares *if and only if* it leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by four. Remainder 1, it splits. Remainder 3, it never will. One digit decides the whole thing. Checked here against every odd prime below two hundred thousand before a word was written: 8,977 split, 9,006 refuse, not one on the wrong side of its remainder.

Why should dividing by four decide anything about squares? Make it geometric. Writing n = a² + b² is the same as landing a whole-number point (a, b) exactly on a circle of radius √n, because a² + b² is that point's squared distance from the origin. So the question becomes: does the circle of radius √n pass through a point of the integer grid? For 13 it threads (2, 3); for 7 it lands on none. One level down sits the real reason, the *Gaussian integers*, numbers a + bi. There a prime that leaves remainder 1 stops being prime: it factors as (a + bi)(a − bi), and multiplying back gives a² + b². A prime that leaves remainder 3 stays prime even there, so no split exists.

slides.sub: Lay the odd primes out coloured by their remainder mod 4, then watch a circle of radius √n hunt for the lattice point that splits n: one point for a prime ≡ 1, none for a prime ≡ 3, several for a composite. Follow it out through the Brahmagupta–Fibonacci identity to Lagrange's promise that four squares is always enough. Every prime is re-sieved and every split re-searched live in your browser on load, nothing stored, nothing to go stale.
